correctness.rationale: For all even n>=4, B>0, r>1, t>0, trace-exp is strictly convex in every independent edge conductance because its symmetric matrix Hessian is positive in every nonzero direction and edge weights determine the Laplacian. Symmetry gives the exact two-class unrestricted optimizer, the pair-antisymmetric and pair-constant eigenspaces give the complete spectrum, and the strictly convex scalar derivative proves the exact b*=0 price-time boundary and interior formula including r=2 and t=T*. Direct algebra yields the diffusive limiting ratio. A standalone verifier passed 17,202 finite checks, corroborating but not replacing this proof.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: For fixed \(1<r<2\), prior gap optimality recommends equal edge rates at all network sizes. The current optimizer instead has matched rates zero for \(t\le T_*\), and positive but strictly lower than ordinary rates for every finite \(t>T_*\). These explicit contradictions to endpoint prescriptions prove that prior optimizer formulas cannot directly imply the entire finite-time answer. At \(r\ge2\), prior gap maximizers can have nonuniform faces, whereas strict heat-trace convexity selects one optimizer.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Trace heat can be viewed as aggregate mean-square diffusion on the centered subspace; this aliases transient consensus error, thermal trace, partition function and Laplacian exponential trace. A spectral-gap maximum does not imply a minimum of the sum of all decay modes at each finite time: in the identified active regime the unique heat optimum is nonuniform even though the spectral-gap optimum is uniform. The fixed graph and full cost budget distinguish this from leader placement or grounded heat traces.

value.rationale: The problem is a natural finite-horizon diffusion resource-allocation design on a complete network with a protected matching of costly links. It yields an exact network-size-dependent activation horizon, a universal price-two permanent-disconnection boundary, and a nontrivial macroscopic positive-part ratio law. It directly distinguishes finite-time whole-spectrum design from preexisting slowest-mode and stationary inverse-trace designs, and strict convexity selects a unique finite-time design even when prior gap problems admit optimizer faces.
